headline: Tufts pause puts prison re-entry students in limbo as university review continues
dek: The university has paused its MyTERN program and its bachelor’s pathway for incarcerated students while in-prison classes continue under a review launched after a former participant was accused in a May shooting.
body: Tufts University has paused its yearlong program for formerly incarcerated students while it reviews the school’s broader prison-education initiative, leaving students and alumni uncertain about the next academic steps. The review followed a May 11 shooting on Memorial Drive involving a former participant, according to a July update from Tufts Provost Joe Auner and reporting by [WBUR](https://www.wbur.org/news/2026/10/02/prison-re-entry-tufts-tyler-brown).

The paused program is the Tufts University Education and Reentry Network, known as MyTERN. WBUR reported that MyTERN offered classes in technology, finance and literature, along with practical help such as housing and employment assistance. Roughly a dozen students received monthly stipends each year, and participants could finish with a civic-engagement certificate and transferable college credits. Those supports made the program more than a classroom: They were intended to help people manage the difficult transition from prison back into work, school and community life.

Tufts’ prison-education initiative, TUPIT, still has an active in-prison component. In its July 9 notice, the university said courses at the Massachusetts Correctional Institution-Shirley would continue and that incarcerated students who had completed associate degrees could keep taking classes at their facilities. The program works with Bunker Hill Community College on associate degrees and with Tufts on bachelor’s study, according to WBUR. The university’s notice is available from the [Office of the Provost](https://provost.tufts.edu/blog/news/2026/07/09/tupit-update/).

The pause affects the path beyond those associate degrees. Tufts said admissions to the bachelor’s program for formerly incarcerated students would remain available through its REAL program, but the university’s August update separately put the bachelor’s pathway for currently incarcerated students on hold while it considered a new admissions approach. The associate’s program is continuing; the bachelor’s route is the part that students and faculty say has become uncertain.

The event that prompted the review remains an allegation, not a court finding. WBUR reported that Tyler Brown, a former MyTERN participant, stopped attending the program in February and was accused of opening fire on drivers along Memorial Drive in May. He has pleaded not guilty to gun-related charges. Neither the university’s review nor the criminal case has established that the program caused the shooting, and the university has not announced a conclusion about Brown’s conduct or the program’s future.

Tufts said the review is meant to examine whether participants have access to appropriate nonacademic supports and whether the program follows university-wide protocols intended to protect students, faculty and staff. Auner convened a working group drawn from the School of Arts and Sciences, Tisch College and the provost’s office. The university also said Melanie MacFarlane, previously the program’s deputy director, replaced founder and executive director Hilary Binda, who would remain as an adviser, according to WBUR.

Students and faculty have challenged the pause and the way decisions were communicated. The [Tufts Daily](https://www.tuftsdaily.com/article/2026/09/students-host-speak-out-on-first-day-of-classes-in-response-to-mytern-suspension-other-changes-to-tupit) reported that students held a speak-out on the first day of fall classes and questioned why people with direct experience in TUPIT were not represented on the working group. Students told the newspaper that the suspension could prevent people who completed associate-level work in prison from moving into the bachelor’s program they had expected to pursue.

The dispute reaches beyond Tufts’ Medford campus. The prison courses are based at MCI-Shirley, while MyTERN served formerly incarcerated people trying to build lives after release in the Boston area. [Open Campus](https://www.opencampus.org/2026/10/02/tufts-pauses-prison-reentry-program-after-shooting-leaving-students-in-limbo/) reported that the program connected students with housing, financial support and employment help, and that Emerson College’s prison-education program has begun welcoming some people with Tufts ties to re-entry workshops. That response shows the immediate gap created when a program pauses without a public timetable for resuming.

Tufts has not said how long the review will take or whether MyTERN and the bachelor’s pathway will return in their previous form. For now, in-prison associate-level classes continue, current students already completing bachelor’s degrees on the Medford-Somerville campus can continue, and the university says it is working to connect participants with other support. The next meaningful update will be the review’s recommendations and a clear decision about whether students inside Shirley can advance toward Tufts degrees and whether formerly incarcerated students will again have a dedicated re-entry bridge after release.
author: NorthEast News Desk
seoTitle: Tufts pauses MyTERN prison re-entry program in Massachusetts
seoDescription: Tufts paused its MyTERN prison re-entry program and bachelor’s pathway while reviewing its prison-education initiative after a May shooting.
